GitHub & The Slow Death of Everything that Once was Great

August 15, 2026

Recently I began the process of moving all of my GitHub repositories to Codeberg. I am far from the only person to be making this move in 2026, if anything, I'm well behind the curve. However, I did want to dedicate a brief essay to detailing (a) how I am conducting my transition to Codeberg, and (b) the reasons why I felt that this move was necessary.

First, for the foreseeable future my intention is to push my public facing repositories, such as my dotfiles, or my Vim2tor project to both GitHub and Codeberg. Largely I view Codeberg as a back-up plan, as I never had any specific gripes with GitHub for the longest time, and still do hope that the site can return to what it in my view once was: a reliably easy place to find, learn about and contribute to open-source software projects. My transition to Codeberg is something that feels thrust upon me rather than a deliberate choice, however, even if GitHub returns to it's former pre-Microsoft and pre-unreliable-AI-slop-farm day, I'll likely still push to both platforms, if for no other reason than to be in compliance with the old prepper one-liner: "Two is one, and one is none."

The process for doing this is very simple:

cd REPO

# Ensure empty repository with the same name has been made on Codeberg, and any required SSH keys have been added to Codeberg

git remote set-url --add --push origin git@codeberg.org:USER/REPO
git remote set-url --add --push origin git@github.com:USER/REPO

And can be confirmed with:

git remote -v

# Example Output
orgin	git@github.com:makccr/dot (fetch)
origin	git@github.com:makccr/dot (push)
origin	git@codeberg.org:makccr/dot (push)

However, if you would like further reading or more details for setting this up with the best practices in mind, I'll refer any readers interested to Schalk Neethling's dedicated guide.

The more interesting question of course here is why the need felt necessary? The easiest answer of course, is simply the unquestionably degraded reliability of the platform. GitHub claims to guarantee 99.9% uptime over the course of a calendar month, any while this goal sounds awesome, GitHub hasn't actually delivered on it in years (if ever). This point alone mandates that I look into having back-up options. Initially this took the form of me spinning of a private Git server on a machine I already had running, but recently it's occurred to me that the proper thing to do, would be to also ensure there is a back-up for the public repositories as well. Codeberg in particular seems like a great choice for this, thanks to their rent commitments to banning both AI generated code & cryptocurrency related projects from their platform, two stances that I am a big fan of, even if I'm unsure exactly how thoroughly these things can realistically be prevented from entering the platform.

This point does however bring up an interesting and worthy point of discussion: the AI and big-business infestation of what used to be trustworthy and helpful projects online. The temptation to blame the constant degradation of online platforms on Artificial Intelligence in The Year of our Lord, 2026 is strong, mostly because AI is to blame for a really big chunk of it. However, there are still examples of projects going downhill, most notably for me at least was Bitwarden a password-manager who's troubles this year have had absolutely nothing to do with forcing AI into the platform. Rather, Bitwarden's unannounced change in leadership earlier this year, and silent fiddling with the GRIT acronym on their website, in a fashion much the same as Google's famous removing "Do No Evil" as their motto; was more than enough to push me to close my Bitwarden account and move to Keepass a few months ago.

The problem is far bigger in indeed than AI: Whether it's Meta buying Instagram and forcing everyone to an Algorithmic timeline when I was in high school, or Amazon buying and slowly making IMDb less and less useful as time goes on, or even by beloved Plex service insisting on shoving their own "free" TV and move services down my throat, and ignoring the fact that I've already added the fact that I've already added anything and everything I'd want to watch to my own server and just user their apps as a front-end to access that content; the list of projects that have blown-up just to blow up is staggering. In my view it has never been more important to be aware of where the tools you are using come from, and who own them. Of course a great place to start is buy trying to shift usage towards open-source software, but even this is not the golden ticket that it used to be. Increasingly then, I have found my posture forced into a position of always having a way out. For just about every service I use to power this website, or just getting through my daily life I've found myself scheming up and documenting an escape plan, my dual pushing to GitHub and Codeberg is simply the first public example of this philosophy.
